kp.k: Legal problem recognition constrains access to justice
kp.d: Hagan argues that unmet civil legal need reflects a recognition gap as well as insufficient service capacity: people describe life problems without identifying their legal dimensions. She reports the LSC’s 2022 findings that 74% of low-income households experience at least one civil legal problem annually and that low-income Americans receive inadequate or no help for 92% of their civil legal problems. She also reports Sandefur’s finding that people characterized only 9% of their civil justice situations as legal. LIST is intended to translate ordinary descriptions into categories usable by search, triage, chatbot and referral systems.

kp.k: Naming provides a framework for technology-assisted issue spotting
kp.d: The paper draws on Felstiner, Abel and Sarat’s 1980 framework of naming, blaming and claiming to explain how experiences become disputes. It reports UK research by Pleasence, Balmer and Denvir associating characterization of problems as legal with possible lawyer engagement increasing from 7% to 9% and handling problems alone dropping from 59% to 44%. Hagan uses these findings to motivate the design question of whether technology can help people recognize legal issues; they are not presented as results of a LIST intervention.

kp.d: Hagan treats digital epidemiology as an analogy for detecting emerging legal needs, monitoring problem patterns, examining help-seeking behavior and analyzing developments preceding disputes. kp.k: LIST combines inherited classifications with iterative expert review
kp.d: The Stanford Legal Design Lab, Suffolk LIT Lab and Pew Charitable Trusts collaboration began exploring taxonomies in 2017 and systematic LIST construction in 2018. The team used NSMI v1, containing nearly 2,000 terms under 58 high-level categories, organizational taxonomies and site maps from 30 US statewide legal help portals. Manual sorting reduced the top level to 20 categories and produced a working draft of approximately 400 codes, typically with 10–20 children per parent. Approximately 20 volunteer reviewers and workshops with legal aid and court professionals informed revisions, including cross-listing and informal user-intent phrases.

kp.k: User-centered standards extend beyond legal aid service categories
kp.d: LIST’s design principles prioritize standalone comprehensibility, usability by non-specialist legal professionals, coverage of the public’s civil legal problems, machine-readability, consistent granularity, responsiveness to ordinary descriptions and interoperability. Hagan argues for including issues such as neighbor disputes, small business problems, online consumer issues and pet custody even when they fall outside customary legal aid case-management categories. The aim is a common classification infrastructure rather than merely a redesigned public interface.

kp.k: Reddit topic modeling identified coverage and taxonomy gaps
kp.d: The team evaluated correspondence with public descriptions using approximately 75,000 Reddit Legal Advice posts. Preliminary classifiers trained on Learned Hands data filtered posts before LDA topic modeling within categories. For family, housing and work/employment, the analysis identified 30–40 main clusters per domain. The paper reports that most clusters matched LIST categories, while gaps included nuanced pay disputes, harassment boundary questions, post-relationship housing and financial problems, pet custody, adult child–parent conflicts, relatives’ wrongdoing and after-death administration. These findings informed extensions and refinements; the evidence concerns this online population.

kp.k: Shared labels support training data and issue classifiers
kp.d: Learned Hands used LIST codes to crowd-label approximately 3,400 Reddit user stories, described by the paper as the largest publicly available dataset of lay legal problem descriptions annotated with standardized issue codes. The dataset supports classifier training and analysis of inter-annotator agreement, including ambiguous issue boundaries. Stanford also developed a curated-keyword classifier, characterized as interpretable and inexpensive but unable to handle paraphrases and novel expressions reliably. As of 2026, the paper reports several legal aid organizations and vendors building or deploying LIST-targeting classifiers, with comparative benchmarking still active work.

kp.k: Common codes connect legal resources and organizational data
kp.d: The paper reports LIST use in statewide legal help portals, including California’s, to tag content and connect classified problems to guides, FAQs and referrals. Service directories can map issue codes to organizations serving those issues. Hagan argues that shared intake codes also enable comparison and aggregation of legal needs across organizations, jurisdictions and time periods, conditional on common adoption. This is an infrastructure capability claim rather than a quantified finding about improved user outcomes.

kp.k: Crosswalks must reconcile distinct legal classification systems
kp.d: The paper distinguishes LIST’s public-facing civil legal aid orientation from SALI LMSS’s commercial legal orientation. It reports SALI’s growth to over 18,000 tags, integrations by Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis, NetDocuments and iManage, and a 2024 API standard. Overlapping territory does not yield simple equivalence: SALI’s faceted structure and LIST’s hierarchy can require many-to-many mappings, while some codes have no counterpart. Local classifications reflect genuine customization needs but create interoperability barriers. Hagan recommends crosswalks combining automated mapping, expert judgment and endorsement by taxonomy stewards.

kp.k: Maintenance and benchmarking require sustained infrastructure investment
kp.d: LIST is maintained primarily by Stanford Legal Design Lab in Airtable and at taxonomy.legal through a largely manual process dependent on a small team. Hagan proposes, rather than reports deployment of, a semi-automated maintenance pipeline that clusters classification failures and low-confidence predictions for expert review. Humans would retain decisions about adding, modifying or reorganizing codes. The paper identifies systematic crosswalks, shared classifier benchmarks using gold-standard labeled data and semi-automated maintenance as urgent priorities, arguing that sustained infrastructure investment must accompany application development.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hagan presents shared legal-issue classifications as infrastructure for AI-assisted issue spotting, legal-help routing, interoperability, and future data-informed maintenance.
pts.d: Hagan argues that LIST can translate lay descriptions of life problems into categories usable by classifiers, search tools, chatbots, triage systems, and referral services. She reports its use as a labeling scheme for classifier training and as a shared vocabulary for connecting problems to legal-help content and organizations. She argues that shared codes support comparison of legal-needs data across organizations and jurisdictions. Looking ahead, she anticipates growing importance for crosswalks connecting LIST, SALI, and local schemes, shared classifier benchmarks to inform deployment decisions, and semi-automated maintenance that surfaces classification gaps for expert review. Drawing an analogy with digital epidemiology, she also proposes potential applications in detecting and monitoring emerging legal needs, rather than reporting these as demonstrated outcomes. The paper does not predict lawyer replacement or quantify AI-driven changes in employment, fees, or market shares.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of taxonomy-construction experience, expert review, exploratory NLP analysis, labeled training data, and reported operational adoption; future benefits are proposals rather than measured service outcomes.
pts.d: Hagan describes building LIST from inherited professional taxonomies, comparing navigation structures from 30 statewide legal-help portals, and incorporating feedback from approximately 20 volunteer reviewers and professional workshops. For empirical coverage evaluation, the team applied LDA topic modeling to subsets of approximately 75,000 Reddit Legal Advice posts, filtered through preliminary classifiers. In family, housing, and employment, it identified 30–40 clusters per domain; most matched existing categories, while others prompted extensions. Learned Hands generated approximately 3,400 labeled user stories used for classifier training and inter-annotator agreement research. Hagan reports portal adoption, including California, and classifier development or deployment by legal aid organizations and vendors. Cited legal-needs surveys establish the recognition gap and unmet need motivating the work, not the effectiveness of AI interventions. The paper supplies no comparative classifier performance scores, measured reductions in unmet legal need, or quantified efficiency gains from the proposed maintenance pipeline.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 2026 paper distinguishes existing infrastructure and applications from prospective improvements dependent on standards, sustained maintenance, benchmarking, and expert judgment.
pts.d: Landscape exploration began in 2017 and systematic LIST construction in 2018. Hagan describes classifiers targeting LIST as being built or deployed as of 2026, with comparative benchmarking still active work. Crosswalking and semi-automated maintenance are future priorities without fixed delivery dates. Interoperability depends on organizations adopting shared codes or supported mappings; crosswalks require technical mapping, expert resolution of ambiguous relationships, and institutional coordination. The existing keyword classifier is characterized as interpretable and inexpensive but unable to handle some paraphrases and novel expressions. Low-confidence classifications are possible signals of taxonomy gaps, not definitive proof. In the envisioned maintenance pipeline, humans retain decisions about adding, modifying, and reorganizing codes. Sustained investment is required because legal issues and public descriptions change over time.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries envisaged are people with unmet civil legal needs and the organizations building or delivering public-facing legal help.
pts.d: For the public, especially people who do not recognize the legal dimensions of housing, debt, employment, or family problems, the intended benefit is better issue recognition and connection to relevant information and services. Legal aid organizations, courts, portal operators, and directory providers gain shared categories for intake, routing, and content matching. Legal technologists and vendors gain target labels and training infrastructure for classifiers. Law students, paralegals, court clerks, and other non-specialists are intended users of comprehensible codes. Funders, policymakers, and researchers could compare patterns of need across organizations and locations. Taxonomy stewards could receive automatically prioritized candidates for updates while retaining expert responsibility. Commercial legal operations and vendors enter the argument through SALI interoperability; Hagan distinguishes that constituency from LIST's civil legal aid and public-help focus.
